Prioritization of Prevention: The Ministry of Health (MOH) has made the prevention and reduction of healthcare-associated infections (HCAIs) a national priority. 3. Improved Monitoring and Accountability: Discussions have been held to integrate evaluation tools into routine hospital monitoring across Tanzania. These tools are also being incorporated into existing quality improvement programs. 4. Community Engagement in Hygiene Committees: In Cameroon’s Southwest Region, where cholera outbreaks have been recurrent since 2003, hygiene committees were established in healthcare facilities located in cholera hotspots. These committees consist of well-trained, multidisciplinary teams capable of responding within 72 hours. Community partnerships were also strengthened, improving adherence to hand hygiene guidelines and disease surveillance. 5. Upgraded WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) Facilities: In treatment centers, wards were refurbished to include isolation areas, increased bed spacing, natural ventilation, lighting systems, and handwashing materials. Disinfection practices for wards and patient transport vehicles were also enhanced. 6. Community-Level WASH Practices: Community sensitization efforts have improved practices related to disinfection, household water treatment, and proper disposal of human waste and food hygiene. 7. Challenges and Opportunities in Cholera Prevention: Despite progress, the risk of cholera resurgence remains high in Cameroon due to its proximity to endemic regions. Continuous community education on hygiene practices is essential, though behavior change and limited funding remain challenges. 8. National WASH Initiatives in Mali: Following a 2012 cholera outbreak, Mali’s Ministry of Health conducted a national assessment of healthcare facilities, revealing significant inadequacies in water supply and sanitation. An intersectoral task force was established to coordinate efforts, leading to the adoption of a minimum national WASH package and the rollout of WASH training programs. Over 200 healthcare facilities have since benefited from infrastructure upgrades. 9. India’s Kayakalp Program: Launched in 2015, this initiative aimed to improve cleanliness, hygiene, waste management, and infection control in public healthcare facilities. Facilities achieving at least 70% of the program’s indicators received cash awards. By 2017, over 500 facilities had been recognized, and specific programs in states like Madhya Pradesh focused on improving WASH in maternity settings, benefiting over 120,000 newborns. 10. Development of WASH Assessment Tools in Kenya: Researchers adapted the WASH FIT tool to create the WASH Facility Survey Tool (WASH-FaST) for assessing larger, more complex healthcare facilities. This tool helped identify quick wins, such as increasing waste bins and improving waste segregation practices. 11. Global Advocacy and Knowledge Sharing: WHO and UNICEF have established a global network to provide technical support and share best practices for improving WASH in healthcare facilities. This includes a knowledge portal with resources, case studies, and tools to support countries in achieving sustainable WASH services. 12. Addressing Global Health Security: WASH services are critical for infection prevention and control, particularly in the context of outbreaks like Ebola and cholera. Climate change, migration, conflict, and urbanization pose additional challenges to health security, emphasizing the need for sustainable WASH solutions. 13. Call to Action: The UN Secretary-General has highlighted the urgency of improving WASH in healthcare facilities, recognizing it as fundamental to infection prevention, quality care, and human dignity. Incremental improvements, collaboration, and multi-sectoral planning are essential to achieving universal access to quality care.
